function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse and the constraints of your experiment.** Below is a quick guide to help you decide which technique might suit your needs best. | Ionisation Technique | Typical Applications | Advantages | Disadvantages | When to Use | |----------------------|----------------------|------------|---------------|-------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Small, volatile, thermally stable molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, pesticides). | • Produces reproducible, highly fragmentary spectra (good library matching).
• Robust, low‑maintenance source. | • Requires high vacuum.
• Not suitable for large or labile molecules. | When you need a standard, well‑characterised fragmentation pattern for database identification. | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Similar to EI but for slightly larger or more polar compounds. | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation.
• Can use reagent gases (CH₄, NH₃) to tune ion chemistry. | • Still requires vacuum.
• Lower sensitivity for very large molecules. | When you want a balance between fragmentation and molecular‑ion detection. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Small to medium‑sized, moderately polar molecules (e.g., pharmaceuticals, steroids). | • Operates at atmospheric pressure → easier sample introduction.
• Good for LC‑MS coupling. | • Less effective for very polar or large biomolecules. | When coupling to LC and analysing moderately polar analytes. | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Large, polar, thermally labile molecules (proteins, peptides, nucleic acids, metabolites). | • Very soft → preserves intact molecular ions.
• Works well with LC‑MS.
• Capable of generating multiply charged ions, extending mass range. | • Requires a liquid sample; not suitable for non‑volatile compounds.
• Can suffer from ion suppression in complex matrices. | When analysing large biomolecules or when you need to detect intact molecular ions. | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteins, peptides, polymers, large biomolecules. | • Handles very large molecules (up to >1 MDa).
• Minimal sample prep (matrix addition).
• High throughput. | • Requires matrix selection; can introduce background peaks.
• Typically single‑charged ions → limited resolution for very large proteins. | When you need to analyse large biomolecules quickly and can tolerate matrix background. | | **Laser Desorption Ionisation (LDI)** | Similar to MALDI but without a matrix (often used for inorganic or polymer samples). | • No matrix background. | • Less efficient for many organic molecules. | When you want to avoid matrix interference. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | Non‑polar, aromatic compounds (e.g., PAHs, PCBs). | • Works well for non‑polar analytes that are difficult for APCI/ESI. | • Requires a UV lamp and sometimes dopants. | When analysing non‑polar, aromatic compounds. | | **Fast Atom Bombardment (FAB)** | Polar, non‑volatile compounds (polysaccharides, peptides). | • Soft ionisation for polar molecules. | • Requires a liquid matrix; limited mass range. | When you need to analyse polar, non‑volatile molecules. | ### How to pick: 1. **Molecular size & polarity** * Small, volatile → EI or CI. * Medium, polar → APCI or ESI. * Large, polar → ESI or MALDI. 2. **Sample state** * Liquid → ESI/APCI/APPI. * Solid or semi‑solid → MALDI/LDI/FAB. 3. **Desired information** * Fragmentation pattern for library ID → EI. * Intact molecular ion → ESI/MALDI. 4. **Instrument compatibility** * If you’re using LC‑MS, ESI/APCI/APPI are the most common. * For GC‑MS, EI/CI are standard. 5. **Sensitivity & matrix effects** * ESI can suffer from ion suppression in complex biological matrices; consider sample cleanup or alternative ionisation (e.g., APCI). * MALDI is less affected by matrix effects but introduces its own background peaks. --- #### Quick Decision Flowchart ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the sample liquid? │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Use ESI/APCI/APPI │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ No → Is it solid? │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Use MALDI/LDI │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ No → Use EI/CI (GC‑MS) │ └───────────────────────┘ ``` --- **Bottom line:** - **ESI** is often the “go‑to” for modern LC‑MS workflows, especially for biomolecules. - **MALDI** excels for very large proteins and polymers. - **EI** remains the gold standard for small, volatile organics in GC‑MS. If you have a specific analyte or application in mind, let me know and I can give a more tailored recommendation!
